newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian SGB rocked by parent, daughter merger talk.
newsitem.headline: Belgian SGB rocked by parent, daughter merger talk.

text.p: The raison d'etre of Ste Generale de Belgique (SGB) is again in question as expected mergers at its French parent and Belgian units squeeze the holding company from both sides, analysts said.
The end of SGB has been forecast more than once in the venerable holding company's 175-year history. So far the company has proved to be a survivor.
But if SGB's French parent Compagnie de Suez, itself a holding company, merges with French utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux, why should SGB escape unscathed?
"If Suez merges with Lyonnaise, it is because it has no reason to exist anymore. It would be logical to follow the same reasoning for SGB," Generale Bank analyst Loic de Caters said.
SGB is 63 percent owned by Suez.
Not only could the cards be reshuffled above its head. SGB is itself expected to be transformed with the merger of two of its main units, while several others are thought up for sale.
Later today, utility group Tractebel SA, 65 percent owned by SGB, is widely expected to announce it will merge with its Powerfin energy unit.
Analysts expect Tractebel to propose a three-for-one merger, which would reduce SGB's stake in the new unit to about 53 percent.
Another object of merger talk is SGB's 30-percent owned Generale Bank unit. SGB has said it would like to see it merge with Banque Bruxelles Lambert.

Analysts said a Generale Bank-BBL merger could cost SGB a lot of money as it tries to avoid its stake in the new entity being diluted to less than 20 percent. Below that level, it would be difficult to consolidate the bank in SGB's earnings.
"I think SGB would try to keep its stake (in a new merged bank) above 20 percent," de Caters said.

Tractebel, Generale Bank and insurer Fortis AG are SGB's three core holdings, in line with Suez-chairman Gerard Mestrallet's focus on utilities and financial services. But most of SGB's other holdings are considered ripe for divestment.

SGB chief executive Philippe Liotier said earlier this month SGB's stakes in non-ferrous metals unit Union Miniere and foam products group Recticel were "not forever". Its stake in steel maker Arbed is officially for sale.
"It is quite possible that by year-end we could see an SGB with just three large financial assets and without debt," said Quentin Quarterman of London-based Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
But does Suez need an intermediate holding structure to manage just three large Belgian assets?
At the presentation of SGB's 1996 earnings on Wednesday, SGB Chairman Etienne Davignon will need more than his usual wit to fend questions about the future of his group.
Analysts have little doubt earnings will be good.

An EFP poll of 11 analysts on Reuters 3000 shows that earnings per share are expected to grow 8.6 percent to 165 francs on average in 1996, with forecasts ranging from 143 to 207 francs. 1997 EPS growth is seen at 17 percent.
Davignon indicated in January the group's dividend would be left unchanged at 87 francs, adding that it would be "technically possible" to consider an optional stock dividend.
Analysts think a stock dividend is likely, as it would allow the debt-laden group to save some eight billion francs in cash.

Davignon said in January SGB had 32 billion francs of debt. Since then, SGB has raised 13.5 billion francs from the sale of its stake in French hotel group Accor and has spent three billion subscribing to a capital increase at Fortis AG. SGB's net debt should be at 20 to 22 billion, analysts said.

If Arbed shares, now at 3,650 francs, rise above 4,000 francs by year-end, SGB could also get another 3.3 to 3.5 billion francs from the exercise of bonds convertible in Arbed shares at 4,000 francs per share.
